string-array.name: municipalities_array
string-array.item: Beijing is the capital of China and one of its four municipalities directly administered by the central government. The municipal government describes it as the country\'s political and cultural center, as well as a hub for international communication and scientific and technological innovation. In northern China, Beijing combines a modern national capital with a long urban history: it served as the capital of the State of Yan during the Western Zhou Dynasty. Its 16 districts range from dense historic neighborhoods to mountain and suburban areas. The Forbidden City, Temple of Heaven, and sections of the Great Wall make the city\'s imperial heritage visible alongside universities, research institutions, and contemporary arts.

Shanghai is a municipality directly administered by China\'s central government, located at the Yangtze River estuary in eastern China and facing the Pacific. It forms part of the Yangtze River Delta and is organized into 16 districts. The city developed as a major port and today is known for finance, shipping, trade, science and technology, and international business. Historic streets and the Bund\'s waterfront architecture sit alongside Pudong\'s modern skyline. Museums, theaters, varied neighborhoods, and local food reflect both Shanghai\'s regional traditions and its long connections with people and commerce from around the world.

Chongqing is a municipality in southwest China on the upper reaches of the Yangtze River. Its area of about 82,400 square kilometers spans rural landscapes as well as a densely built urban core. The city rises among hills and river valleys, where the Yangtze and Jialing rivers meet, creating steep streets, layered neighborhoods, bridges, and elevated views. Chongqing is an important regional center for transport, manufacturing, commerce, and culture. Its location links western China with the Yangtze corridor and the Three Gorges. Hot-pot traditions, historic sites, and lively night scenes add to its reputation as a distinctive mountain city.

Tianjin is a municipality directly administered by China\'s central government in northern China, near Beijing and the Bohai Sea. Its alluvial plain and network of rivers helped it grow into a transportation and trading hub connecting inland routes with coastal shipping. The city\'s recorded establishment dates to 1404, when the Ming government set up the Tianjin Garrison; its name is often interpreted as meaning a ford used by the emperor. Tianjin later became a gateway for northern maritime commerce and remains an important port and industrial center. Today, the Haihe waterfront, historic neighborhoods, museums, and local foods reveal layers of trade and urban life.
